title: FASTER: Fast Adjoint Stochastic Transport for Endpoint Refinement in Reward-Guided Image Editing

paper.title: FASTER: Fast Adjoint Stochastic Transport for Endpoint Refinement in Reward-Guided Image Editing
paper.abstract: Abstract Reward-guided image editing at test time seeks to improve a specified reward while preserving source content and visual plausibility. Many existing approaches optimize candidates through pretrained generation processes, making repeated adjustment depend on costly large-model execution and, in some cases, backbone backpropagation. We develop a theoretical framework that jointly accounts for reward, source preservation, and pretrained-prior preferences, allowing the desired output distribution to be specified separately from the dynamics used to realize it. Based on this framework, we introduce FASTER, which trains a small network for each source and objective to perform inexpensive editing, while pretrained and reward models provide feedback on candidate outputs. By reusing each candidate and its feedback across multiple small-network updates, FASTER reduces repeated sampling and supervision queries without placing the pretrained generative backbone inside the inner optimization loop. On SD3, FASTER leads all four target metrics and several validation metrics among the evaluated methods. Compared with the evaluated baseline that optimizes controls along pretrained generation trajectories, FASTER achieves editing-time speedups of up to 6.91 × {6.91\times} on Stable Diffusion 3 and 24.14 × {24.14\times} on Stable Diffusion 1.5.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Decoupling pretrained knowledge from editing dynamics. (a) Trajectory optimization repeatedly executes a frozen generative backbone. (b) FASTER learns a small per-image editor at test time, reusing frozen-model feedback across updates; the learned network then performs the edit. Pretrained diffusion and flow models provide rich visual priors for image generation ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . However, their conditioning interfaces do not fully express every downstream objective: human preferences, reference styles, and task-specific semantic requirements may instead be specified through rewards available at test time. Reward-guided inference adapts generated outputs to such objectives without retraining the pretrained model ( Bansal et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Susladkar et al., 2026 ) . We focus on reward-guided image editing at test time : given a source image and a reward objective, improve the objective while retaining content that need not change and maintaining visual plausibility ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . Unlike unconstrained reward maximization, this task requires meaningful, source-preserving changes; a higher reward alone does not establish a successful edit. Existing approaches typically inject reward guidance into pretrained generation or optimize candidates through a generation mapping or trajectory. Guidance methods use external gradients to adjust intermediate states, with refinements to the guidance geometry and update rules ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ; Susladkar et al., 2026 ) . Optimization-based approaches instead adjust input noise, editable variables, or trajectory controls to improve the generated output ( Wallace et al., 2023 ; Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Chang et al., 2026 ) . Other advances improve efficiency through reward optimization of one-step models, flow-based editing, or efficient reward guidance ( Eyring et al., 2024 ; Patel et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Despite their different computational costs, many of these approaches couple the pretrained model’s role as a source of visual knowledge with its role in executing candidate updates. Repeated adjustment invokes the generator again, and some approaches additionally backpropagate through its backbone; candidate evaluation introduces further decoding and reward-computation costs. Can pretrained knowledge continue to constrain desirable edits while a separate, lightweight process performs the actual adjustment? Figure 1 contrasts optimization along pretrained generation trajectories with FASTER’s lightweight editing process: the former repeatedly executes the large generative backbone, whereas the latter uses a small network to perform editing with feedback from frozen models. We establish a theoretical basis for this separation by jointly analyzing reward improvement, source preservation, and pretrained-prior plausibility, specifying a target output distribution and constructing an independent editing process that realizes it under ideal conditions. Each task fixes a source and an objective, so the learned editor need only adapt the current instance rather than acquire general-purpose generation capabilities. Based on this framework, we introduce FASTER : a small network trained at test time performs inexpensive editing updates, while pretrained and reward models provide feedback at candidate outputs. Reusing each candidate and its feedback across multiple network updates reduces repeated sampling and costly supervision queries. To support explicit semantic changes that increasing an image–text score may fail to produce, we further introduce an editing term that obtains semantic directions from the pretrained model’s conditional predictions, without backpropagation through its backbone. This term enters the same feedback interface, allowing the lightweight editor to use pretrained semantic knowledge while retaining its inexpensive update process. On Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , FASTER leads the target metric in all four tasks and several validation metrics among the evaluated methods. Relative to the evaluated baseline that optimizes controls along pretrained generation trajectories, it achieves editing-time speedups of up to 6.91 × 6.91\times on Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and 24.14 × 24.14\times on Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Our contributions are threefold: • Decoupling the editing target from its dynamics. We combine reward, source preservation, and pretrained-prior preferences into a target distribution, and construct separate lightweight dynamics that realize it under proper conditions theoretically. • FASTER: inexpensive editing with a small network. A per-image small network executes inexpensive edits and reuses candidate feedback to reduce repeated computation. A semantic editing term supplies directions from conditional model predictions through the same interface, without generative-backbone backpropagation. • Editing quality and efficiency across tasks. FASTER leads all four target metrics and several validation metrics in the SD3 comparison, with up to 6.91 × \bm{6.91\times} and 24.14 × \bm{24.14\times} speedups on SD3 and SD1.5, respectively. A 768 × 768 768\times 768 SD3 ImageReward edit takes approximately 7.7 7.7 seconds on a single consumer GPU.

sections.heading: Inference-time guidance and alignment.
sections.text: Training-free guidance steers pretrained diffusion and flow models toward external objectives without updating model weights. DPS, Universal Guidance, and FreeDoM construct guidance from denoised predictions or external energies ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ) , while MPGD, DSG, and TFG further improve the geometry and design of guidance ( He et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) . Alternatively, DOODL and D-Flow optimize latent variables through the pretrained generative mapping ( Wallace et al., 2023 ; Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) , with DNO and ReNO improving robustness or efficiency of direct optimization ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ) . Distributional methods such as DAS and Feynman–Kac steering instead reshape inference through reweighting and resampling ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . These approaches provide flexible test-time alignment, but generally remain coupled to pretrained generation during optimization.

sections.heading: Training-free and reward-guided image editing.
sections.text: Training-free image editing must also preserve source correspondence. Existing methods use inversion and attention control ( Hertz et al., 2023b ; Mokady et al., 2023 ) , controlled corruption ( Meng et al., 2022 ) , and feature reuse ( Tumanyan et al., 2023 ; Cao et al., 2023 ) . Other approaches rely on score differences ( Hertz et al., 2023a ) or directly model source-to-target editing dynamics ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Kulikov et al., 2025 ) . For reward-guided editing, ITOC optimizes controls along the pretrained trajectory ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . FlowChef exploits flow geometry ( Patel et al., 2025 ) , whereas RewardFlow combines multiple differentiable rewards ( Susladkar et al., 2026 ) . FMRG further improves guidance efficiency through flow-map lookahead ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . FASTER instead specifies a source-conditioned endpoint target and learns a separate lightweight transport to realize it.

sections.heading: Generative priors and stochastic-control optimization.
sections.text: Frozen models provide priors for inverse imaging ( Feng et al., 2023 ; Feng & Bouman, 2024 ; Mardani et al., 2024 ) and score-distillation-based 3D optimization ( Poole et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . UniDB formulates diffusion bridges as SOC with a tunable terminal penalty ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , while UniDB++ accelerates sampling within this framework through a training-free solver ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . For SOC solvers, Adjoint Matching learns controls by regression ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) , Adjoint Sampling reuses terminal information through reference bridges ( Havens et al., 2025 ) , and Efficient Adjoint Matching simplifies the reference dynamics and terminal cost ( Shin et al., 2026 ) . FASTER uses frozen-model endpoint supervision to learn a lightweight per-image editor.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Following Chang et al. (2026) , we evaluate four reward-guided editing tasks with 300 source–condition pairs each. Human preference optimizes ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . Style transfer minimizes the Gram-matrix difference between output and reference-image features from CLIP ViT-B/16 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . Counterfactual generation maximizes the target-class logit of a robust ResNet-50 classifier ( Engstrom et al., 2019 ) , using a class label as the reward condition. Text-guided facial editing maximizes CLIP ViT-L/14 image–text similarity for the requested attribute. Each task also reports validation metrics not directly optimized: HPSv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , CLIPScore, and Aesthetic for human preference; reference-image CLIP-I and DINO ( Caron et al., 2021 ) similarity for style; target-class text CLIPScore for counterfactual generation; and ImageReward and HPSv2 for facial editing. These metrics assess whether target improvements generalize beyond the optimized reward. We use Stable Diffusion 3 Medium (SD3) ( Esser et al., 2024 ) for the main quality comparison. The baselines are ITOC ( Chang et al., 2026 ) , gradient ascent (GA), DPS ( Chung et al., 2023 ) , FreeDoM ( Yu et al., 2023 ) , TFG ( Ye et al., 2024 ) , and MPGD ( He et al., 2024 ) ; GA performs gradient ascent in latent space. Appendix F details the datasets, reward models, evaluation protocol, and baseline implementations, and provides the SD1.5 results.

sections.heading: 5.1 Main Results

Facial editing similarly combines the highest target CLIPScore with the best ImageReward. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced a decoupled view of reward-guided image editing at test time, in which pretrained models provide visual knowledge while a separate lightweight process executes the edit. Our theoretical framework jointly accounts for reward improvement, source preservation, and prior preferences, establishing a basis for specifying desirable outputs independently of pretrained generation trajectories. Building on this framework, FASTER trains a small per-image network and reuses candidate outputs and their costly feedback across multiple inexpensive updates. A complementary editing term obtains semantic directions from conditional model predictions without backpropagating through the pretrained backbone, supporting changes that image–text score maximization alone may fail to produce. Across four tasks, FASTER achieves competitive target and independent validation metrics, with editing-time speedups of up to 6.91 × 6.91\times on SD3 and 24.14 × 24.14\times on SD1.5 relative to the evaluated baseline that optimizes controls along pretrained generation trajectories.

sections.text: With K K endpoint refreshes and one candidate per refresh, the basic loop computes K K endpoint targets, up to the chosen number of noisy-score samples per candidate. Its K ​ M KM controller updates reuse those targets and draw new bridge times and noises. Each refresh also requires N N evaluations of the small controller for Euler–Maruyama simulation. sections.heading: Frozen inputs.
sections.text: We instantiate the four tasks of Chang et al. (2026) with 300 frozen source/condition pairs per task. Human-preference sources use prompts from the Reward Feedback Learning (ReFL) data released with ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) ; style sources are from the Pick-a-Pic test split ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and are paired with five fixed style-reference images; counterfactual sources are ImageNet-1k images ( Deng et al., 2009 ) ; facial-edit sources are CelebA-HQ images ( Karras et al., 2018 ) with single-attribute text requests. All methods for a given model/task use the same source-image hashes, target text or class, and style reference when applicable. For counterfactual targets, we select a nearby ImageNet class using a WordNet IS-A graph ( Miller, 1995 ) .

sections.heading: Baseline implementations.
sections.text: • ITOC ( Chang et al., 2026 ) iteratively optimizes an image-conditioned sampling trajectory using reward adjoints. • Gradient Ascent (GA) directly updates the editable latent using the task-reward gradient. • DPS ( Chung et al., 2023 ) applies posterior-style reward guidance during reverse sampling after source inversion. This is the source-editing adaptation used in the ITOC comparison suite. • FreeDoM ( Yu et al., 2023 ) uses its training-free energy guidance after source inversion, with the same frozen source set. • TFG ( Ye et al., 2024 ) uses training-free reward guidance during the corresponding inversion-conditioned reverse trajectory. • MPGD ( He et al., 2024 ) updates a predicted clean endpoint with the reward gradient. On SD1.5 we use an MPGD-LDM source-edit variant; on SD3 we use a flow-edit adaptation. The model, source set, task reward, and evaluator are paired within each comparison. Differences in inversion and guidance mechanisms are intrinsic to the baselines. We report mean metric values.

sections.heading: Target and validation definitions.
sections.text: Human preference directly optimizes ImageReward and additionally reports HPSv2, image–text CLIPScore ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) , computed as the cosine similarity of CLIP ViT-L/14 image and text embeddings, and Aesthetic. Style directly minimizes the released positive GramDiff and validates with CLIP-I similarity to the style reference and DINO ViT-S/16 similarity. Counterfactual editing optimizes the robust classifier’s target-class logit and validates with CLIPScore for the target-class text. Facial editing optimizes CLIPScore for the attribute request and validates with ImageReward and HPSv2. Source preservation is additionally available as LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and source–output CLIP-I in the per-image evaluator records; these auxiliary columns are kept separate from the target/validation tables. The reward implementations use ImageReward-v1.0 ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14 for image–text cosine similarity ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , and the robust ResNet-50 checkpoint imagenet_l2_3_0.pt distributed with the robustness library ( Engstrom et al., 2019 ) . The counterfactual reward is the target logit, not a target-text score. Style GramDiff uses non-class tokens from hidden_states[2] of openai/clip-vit-base-patch16 ; the optimization reward is the negative Frobenius difference between the output and reference Gram matrices, scaled by 1 / 100 1/100 . The table reports the corresponding positive difference. DINO validation uses ViT-S/16 ( Caron et al., 2021 ) ; HPSv2 follows Wu et al. (2023) . The Aesthetic evaluator uses the released CLIP-feature predictor from https://github.com/christophschuhmann/improved-aesthetic-predictor .

sections.text: Every model–task comparison uses the same 300 source–condition pairs for all seven methods. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.04538v1 [cs.CV] 03 Oct 2026 FASTER: Fast Adjoint Stochastic Transport for Endpoint Refinement in Reward-Guided Image Editing Yimiao Zhou Affiliation: ShanghaiTech UniversityShanghai, China Email: zhouym2025@shanghaitech.edu.cn Zejia Zhong 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: ShanghaiTech UniversityShanghai, China Email: zhongzj2025@shanghaitech.edu.cn Jingya Wang Affiliation: ShanghaiTech UniversityShanghai, China Email: wangjingya@shanghaitech.edu.cn Ye Shi Email: shiye@shanghaitech.edu.cn Abstract Reward-guided image editing at test time seeks to improve a specified reward while preserving source content and visual plausibility. Many existing approaches optimize candidates through pretrained generation processes, making repeated adjustment depend on costly large-model execution and, in some cases, backbone backpropagation. We develop a theoretical framework that jointly accounts for reward, source preservation, and pretrained-prior preferences, allowing the desired output distribution to be specified separately from the dynamics used to realize it. Based on this framework, we introduce FASTER, which trains a small network for each source and objective to perform inexpensive editing, while pretrained and reward models provide feedback on candidate outputs. By reusing each candidate and its feedback across multiple small-network updates, FASTER reduces repeated sampling and supervision queries without placing the pretrained generative backbone inside the inner optimization loop. On SD3, FASTER leads all four target metrics and several validation metrics among the evaluated methods. Compared with the evaluated baseline that optimizes controls along pretrained generation trajectories, FASTER achieves editing-time speedups of up to 6.91 × {6.91\times} on Stable Diffusion 3 and 24.14 × {24.14\times} on Stable Diffusion 1.5. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Decoupling pretrained knowledge from editing dynamics. (a) Trajectory optimization repeatedly executes a frozen generative backbone. (b) FASTER learns a small per-image editor at test time, reusing frozen-model feedback across updates; the learned network then performs the edit. Pretrained diffusion and flow models provide rich visual priors for image generation ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . However, their conditioning interfaces do not fully express every downstream objective: human preferences, reference styles, and task-specific semantic requirements may instead be specified through rewards available at test time. Reward-guided inference adapts generated outputs to such objectives without retraining the pretrained model ( Bansal et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Susladkar et al., 2026 ) . We focus on reward-guided image editing at test time : given a source image and a reward objective, improve the objective while retaining content that need not change and maintaining visual plausibility ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . Unlike unconstrained reward maximization, this task requires meaningful, source-preserving changes; a higher reward alone does not establish a successful edit. Existing approaches typically inject reward guidance into pretrained generation or optimize candidates through a generation mapping or trajectory. Guidance methods use external gradients to adjust intermediate states, with refinements to the guidance geometry and update rules ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ; Susladkar et al., 2026 ) . Optimization-based approaches instead adjust input noise, editable variables, or trajectory controls to improve the generated output ( Wallace et al., 2023 ; Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Chang et al., 2026 ) . Other advances improve efficiency through reward optimization of one-step models, flow-based editing, or efficient reward guidance ( Eyring et al., 2024 ; Patel et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Despite their different computational costs, many of these approaches couple the pretrained model’s role as a source of visual knowledge with its role in executing candidate updates. Repeated adjustment invokes the generator again, and some approaches additionally backpropagate through its backbone; candidate evaluation introduces further decoding and reward-computation costs. Can pretrained knowledge continue to constrain desirable edits while a separate, lightweight process performs the actual adjustment? Figure 1 contrasts optimization along pretrained generation trajectories with FASTER’s lightweight editing process: the former repeatedly executes the large generative backbone, whereas the latter uses a small network to perform editing with feedback from frozen models. We establish a theoretical basis for this separation by jointly analyzing reward improvement, source preservation, and pretrained-prior plausibility, specifying a target output distribution and constructing an independent editing process that realizes it under ideal conditions. Each task fixes a source and an objective, so the learned editor need only adapt the current instance rather than acquire general-purpose generation capabilities. Based on this framework, we introduce FASTER : a small network trained at test time performs inexpensive editing updates, while pretrained and reward models provide feedback at candidate outputs. Reusing each candidate and its feedback across multiple network updates reduces repeated sampling and costly supervision queries. To support explicit semantic changes that increasing an image–text score may fail to produce, we further introduce an editing term that obtains semantic directions from the pretrained model’s conditional predictions, without backpropagation through its backbone. This term enters the same feedback interface, allowing the lightweight editor to use pretrained semantic knowledge while retaining its inexpensive update process. On Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , FASTER leads the target metric in all four tasks and several validation metrics among the evaluated methods. Relative to the evaluated baseline that optimizes controls along pretrained generation trajectories, it achieves editing-time speedups of up to 6.91 × 6.91\times on Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and 24.14 × 24.14\times on Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Our contributions are threefold: • Decoupling the editing target from its dynamics. We combine reward, source preservation, and pretrained-prior preferences into a target distribution, and construct separate lightweight dynamics that realize it under proper conditions theoretically. • FASTER: inexpensive editing with a small network. A per-image small network executes inexpensive edits and reuses candidate feedback to reduce repeated computation. A semantic editing term supplies directions from conditional model predictions through the same interface, without generative-backbone backpropagation. • Editing quality and efficiency across tasks. FASTER leads all four target metrics and several validation metrics in the SD3 comparison, with up to 6.91 × \bm{6.91\times} and 24.14 × \bm{24.14\times} speedups on SD3 and SD1.5, respectively. A 768 × 768 768\times 768 SD3 ImageReward edit takes approximately 7.7 7.7 seconds on a single consumer GPU. 2 Related Work Inference-time guidance and alignment. Training-free guidance steers pretrained diffusion and flow models toward external objectives without updating model weights. DPS, Universal Guidance, and FreeDoM construct guidance from denoised predictions or external energies ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Bansal et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ) , while MPGD, DSG, and TFG further improve the geometry and design of guidance ( He et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) . Alternatively, DOODL and D-Flow optimize latent variables through the pretrained generative mapping ( Wallace et al., 2023 ; Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) , with DNO and ReNO improving robustness or efficiency of direct optimization ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ) . Distributional methods such as DAS and Feynman–Kac steering instead reshape inference through reweighting and resampling ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . These approaches provide flexible test-time alignment, but generally remain coupled to pretrained generation during optimization. Training-free and reward-guided image editing. Training-free image editing must also preserve source correspondence. Existing methods use inversion and attention control ( Hertz et al., 2023b ; Mokady et al., 2023 ) , controlled corruption ( Meng et al., 2022 ) , and feature reuse ( Tumanyan et al., 2023 ; Cao et al., 2023 ) . Other approaches rely on score differences ( Hertz et al., 2023a ) or directly model source-to-target editing dynamics ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Kulikov et al., 2025 ) . For reward-guided editing, ITOC optimizes controls along the pretrained trajectory ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . FlowChef exploits flow geometry ( Patel et al., 2025 ) , whereas RewardFlow combines multiple differentiable rewards ( Susladkar et al., 2026 ) . FMRG further improves guidance efficiency through flow-map lookahead ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . FASTER instead specifies a source-conditioned endpoint target and learns a separate lightweight transport to realize it. Generative priors and stochastic-control optimization. Frozen models provide priors for inverse imaging ( Feng et al., 2023 ; Feng & Bouman, 2024 ; Mardani et al., 2024 ) and score-distillation-based 3D optimization ( Poole et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . UniDB formulates diffusion bridges as SOC with a tunable terminal penalty ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , while UniDB++ accelerates sampling within this framework through a training-free solver ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . For SOC solvers, Adjoint Matching learns controls by regression ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) , Adjoint Sampling reuses terminal information through reference bridges ( Havens et al., 2025 ) , and Efficient Adjoint Matching simplifies the reference dynamics and terminal cost ( Shin et al., 2026 ) . (2026) , we evaluate four reward-guided editing tasks with 300 source–condition pairs each. Human preference optimizes ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . The dotted vertical line marks K = 20 K=20 . 6 Conclusion We introduced a decoupled view of reward-guided image editing at test time, in which pretrained models provide visual knowledge while a separate lightweight process executes the edit. Our theoretical framework jointly accounts for reward improvement, source preservation, and prior preferences, establishing a basis for specifying desirable outputs independently of pretrained generation trajectories. Building on this framework, FASTER trains a small per-image network and reuses candidate outputs and their costly feedback across multiple inexpensive updates. A complementary editing term obtains semantic directions from conditional model predictions without backpropagating through the pretrained backbone, supporting changes that image–text score maximization alone may fail to produce. Across four tasks, FASTER achieves competitive target and independent validation metrics, with editing-time speedups of up to 6.91 × 6.91\times on SD3 and 24.14 × 24.14\times on SD1.5 relative to the evaluated baseline that optimizes controls along pretrained generation trajectories.
